food.text: British cuisine is said to have its roots in the cooking practices of the indigenous Celts. Celtic agriculture and animal breeding produced a wide variety of foodstuffs, such as grain, fruit, vegetables, and cattle.
Roman colonists were able to grow wine in vineyards as far north as Northamptonshire and Lincolnshire. The longevity of Roman occupation is credited with creating the wine industry in Britain.
Seafood was important to the Roman diet, and this led to its increasing popularity in Britain. Shellfish such as oysters were particularly favoured.
Ancient Celts fermented apples to produce cider. This was recorded by Julius Caesar during his attempted invasions of Britain in 55-54 BC.
Strabo records that Celtic Britons cultivated millet, herbs, and root vegetables. They also practised apiculture to produce honey.

Trade with Celtic Gauls in what is now modern-day France and the Low Countries introduced grains such as wheat, oats, and rye to Britain. Trade with the Roman Republic following its conquest of Gaul did the same.
The quality of oysters from Colchester in particular became prized in Rome as a delicacy. This followed the growing popularity of seafood, especially shellfish, in Roman Britain.
Broad beans, wild spinach, herbs, and primitive parsnips were the primary sources of vegetables and greens in Celtic Britain. Strabo also records that root vegetables were cultivated there.

After the end of Roman rule in Britain and the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, the use of more exotic food items lessened. Cooking then predominately consisted of vegetables, cereals, and meats such as mutton.
In Celtic Britain, barley was grown to produce porridge and malt for beer. Flax was also grown there for its oil.

art.text: In the Iron Age, France yielded many of the most impressive finds of early Celtic art. This makes the region one of the important homes of Celtic artistic tradition.

The Gallo-Roman period left a distinctive provincial style of sculpture. The region around the modern Franco-German border also led the Roman Empire in mass-producing finely decorated pottery, which was exported to Italy and elsewhere on a large scale.

Iron Age Britain built defensive earthworks known as hill forts, such as Maiden Castle and Cadbury Castle. Together with burial monuments, they are among the numerous Bronze Age and Iron Age structures still visible in England.

In France, the Hallstatt culture of about 1200 to 500 BC marked the transition into the Iron Age, from which a continental Celtic art developed, mainly associated with the La Tène culture that followed and produced many of the most impressive finds of early Celtic art.

The arrival of the Merovingian dynasty in Gaul in the fifth century changed the arts. Builders no longer aimed for robust and harmonious buildings, and sculpture regressed to little more than ornament for sarcophagi, altars and church furniture.
Archaeological evidence suggests that British Iron Age domestic architecture tended toward circular dwellings, known as roundhouses. They stood alongside the hill forts that defended the landscape.

England's Bronze Age and Iron Age burial monuments took two forms. Individual barrows, also called tumuli, are marked on modern Ordnance Survey maps, and cists covered by cairns are occasionally found.

In fifth-century Gaul, the rise of gold work and manuscript illumination brought a resurgence of Celtic decoration. Combined with Christian and other contributions, it formed the basis of Merovingian art.

Under Clovis I, who lived from 465 to 511, the unified Frankish kingdom needed churches. Their plans were probably copied from Roman basilicas, but the timber buildings did not survive because fire destroyed them, whether by accident or by the Normans.

war.text: At Alesia in September 52 BC, Julius Caesar's army besieged the Gallic leader Vercingetorix and his forces, who numbered about 80,000 men besides the local civilians, intending to starve them into surrender. The Romans built two lines of fortifications, an inner wall to keep the Gauls in and an outer wall to keep a Gallic relief force out, and set the ground in front with concealed pits holding sharpened stakes and with stakes tied in rows so that attackers would be impaled. When food ran short, the Gauls sent out their old and sick, along with wives and children, hoping Caesar would take them captive and feed them. Caesar refused to admit them, and Vercingetorix left them between the lines to starve to death. The battle ended Gallic independence in modern France and Belgium.

In AD 60 or 61, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt against Roman rule in Britain, after the Romans ignored Prasutagus's will, seized lands and enslaved Iceni; according to Tacitus, Boudica was publicly flogged and her daughters raped. Her army destroyed Camulodunum, Verulamium and Londinium, and between seventy and eighty thousand people are said to have been killed in the three settlements. The Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus, though heavily outnumbered, decisively defeated the Britons in a final battle, in which Tacitus says little less than eighty thousand Britons fell, against some four hundred Romans killed.

Hadrian's Wall was begun in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian and ran from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway. It was a stone wall with large ditches in front and behind, garrisoned in forts, milecastles and turrets. It stretched across the whole width of the island.

The Roman conquest of Britain began in earnest in AD 43 under Emperor Claudius, with an army recruited in Italia, Hispania and Gaul and carried by the newly formed fleet Classis Britannica. Under Aulus Plautius it pushed inland from the southeast, defeating the Britons in the Battle of the Medway, which raged for two days, and Roman losses mounted in the marshes of Essex as they pursued the British across the Thames. By AD 47 the Romans held the lands southeast of the Fosse Way.

Vercingetorix, chieftain of the Arverni, united a coalition of Gallic tribes against Caesar in 52 BC. After a cavalry setback he avoided open battle and adopted a scorched-earth strategy: settlements, crops and stores were destroyed to deprive the Romans of supplies, while mobile forces harassed Caesar's foragers. At Avaricum the Romans then captured the city in a sudden assault and massacred the population; of about 40 000 reported inhabitants, only some 800 escaped to Vercingetorix's camp. A Roman defeat at Gergovia nearly brought Caesar to overall defeat and withdrawal from Gaul.

According to Tacitus, the Caledonians were forced to fight at Mons Graupius in AD 83 or 84 when the Romans marched on their main granaries just after harvest. The Caledonians had to fight or starve over the winter. Tacitus says their army, said to be led by Calgacus, was over 30,000 strong.

Mona, now Anglesey, was a stronghold of the druids and a refuge for fugitives. When Suetonius Paulinus landed there in 60 or 61 CE, he faced a mass of armed warriors, Druids and black-clad women waving torches. The Romans rallied and won a brutal victory, smiting down all resistance and wrapping the foe in the flames of his own brands, then destroyed the sacred groves, which Tacitus says were used to cover altars with the blood of captives and to consult the gods through human entrails. He had to withdraw because of the Boudican revolt, and in 77 CE Agricola's thorough subjugation of the island left it under Roman rule.

The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains took place on 20 June 451 AD. A coalition led by the Roman general Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I fought the Huns under Attila, and every primary source calls it exceptionally bloody. Jordanes puts the dead at 165,000 and Hydatius at 300,000, figures the article calls implausibly high, and Theodoric was slain in the fighting. It was one of the last major military operations of the Western Roman Empire, though Germanic foederati made up most of the coalition army.

At Alesia, Caesar's troops built a ring of fortifications 15 km long around the town in only six weeks. They added a second ring 21 km long outside it to stop reinforcements, which Caesar put at around 250,000 men, from reaching the Gauls.

When news of the Boudican rebellion reached Suetonius, he hurried through hostile territory to Londinium. With too few troops, and chastened by Petillius's defeat, he decided to sacrifice the city to save the province. He took with him the citizens who wished to escape and withdrew to regroup his forces, leaving the rest of the inhabitants to their fate. Tacitus says those who stayed were cut off by the enemy, and the rebels burned Londinium, torturing and killing everyone who had not evacuated with him.

According to Cassius Dio, Boudica began her revolt with divination, releasing a hare from the folds of her dress and interpreting the direction in which it ran. She also invoked Andraste, a British goddess of victory.

In AD 40, Caligula assembled 200,000 men at the Channel for an invasion of Britain. According to Suetonius, they were only made to gather seashells, perhaps as a symbolic gesture proclaiming Caligula's victory over the sea. Claudius invaded successfully three years later.

literature.text: Julius Caesar wrote a first-hand account of his campaigns in Gaul, the Commentarii de Bello Gallico, as a third-person narrative. It describes the nine years he spent fighting the Celtic and Germanic peoples who opposed Roman conquest. Caesar claimed the Romans faced a Gallic army of 430,000 and lost not a single soldier, and that the Gauls then committed mass suicide; historians such as David Henige find this impossible. The work also has Caesar describe Druids burning people alive in giant wicker figures, and it has long been a mainstay in Latin instruction because of its simple, direct prose.

The Vindolanda tablets are postcard-sized wooden leaf-tablets written with carbon-based ink, dating to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD. Robin Birley discovered the first ones in 1973 at a Roman fort in northern England. As of 2023, more than 1,700 tablets have been found.

Ogham is an alphabet used to write early Irish, with roughly 400 surviving orthodox inscriptions on stone monuments across Ireland and western Britain. The Munster counties of Cork and Kerry contain 60% of all Irish ogham stones. The inscriptions usually consist of personal names written in a set formula.

Ausonius, a Roman poet and teacher of rhetoric from Burdigala (now Bordeaux), wrote Mosella, a description of the River Moselle, and Ephemeris, an account of a typical day in his life. He was tutor to the future Emperor Gratian, who afterwards bestowed the consulship on him.

Around 100, Claudia Severa, wife of the commander of a nearby fort, wrote Tablet 291 to Sulpicia Lepidina, inviting her to a birthday party. It is one of the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman. Most of the text is in a professional hand, thought to be the household scribe, while Claudia Severa added the closing greetings herself.

The Bloomberg tablets, 405 preserved wooden tablets found in London, are the earliest written documents found in Britain, dating from 50 to 80 AD. They predate the Vindolanda tablets, which had previously been the earliest writing examples found in Britain.

Sidonius Apollinaris was honored for his poetry, including panegyrics on emperors, with a bronze statue in the libraries of Trajan's Forum. A large number of his letters also survive, making him 'the single most important surviving author from 5th-century Gaul' according to Eric Goldberg.

Early in the fifth century AD the poet Claudian praised the conquests of the emperor Theodosius I in a poem on the Fourth Consulship of the Emperor Honorius. He wrote that the Orcades "ran red with Saxon slaughter", that Thule "was warm with the blood of Picts", and that ice-bound Hibernia wept for the heaps of slain Scots. Readers took this to mean Thule was Scotland.

One Bloomberg tablet contains the first mention of the name of the city of London. This is more than half a century earlier than the Annals of Tacitus, which had previously been thought to hold the first naming of London.

Archaeological evidence dates the earliest ogham inscriptions to about the 4th century AD. Yet some letters stand for sounds no longer spoken by the 5th century and never appear in inscriptions, suggesting an extended period of ogham writing on wood or other perishable material beforehand.

When Gratian became emperor in 375, Ausonius was made Praetorian Prefect of Gaul. After campaigning against the Alemanni he received a slave girl, Bissula, as part of his booty, and he addressed a poem to her.

Most scholars favour the Latin alphabet as the template for ogham, mainly because it was widely used in neighbouring Roman Britannia in the 4th century. The Elder Futhark and even the Greek alphabet have their supporters, and a runic origin would explain the unused letters H and Z.

A letter of Sidonius Apollinaris addressed to Riothamus, 'King of the Brittones', dates to about 470. It is of particular interest because it provides evidence that a king or military leader with ties to Britain lived around the time frame of King Arthur.

The fourth-century commentator Servius, who wrote about Virgil, placed Thule in the Ocean beyond Britain, near Orkney and Ireland. He noted that when the sun is in Cancer, it is said there are perpetual days without nights there.

science.text: Around 325 BC, Pytheas, a Greek from the colony of Massalia (modern Marseille), sailed to Northern Europe and visited a considerable part of the British Isles. He was the first known Greek scientific visitor to describe the Arctic and polar ice. He is also the first person on record to describe the midnight sun.

The Coligny calendar is a bronze plaque made in Roman Gaul in the 2nd century CE. It lays out a 5-year cycle of a lunisolar calendar, with 12 lunar months in each year. An intercalary month is inserted before each 2.5 years, and the plaque is the most important evidence for reconstructing an ancient Celtic calendar.

Pytheas's account of the tides is the earliest known one that suggests the moon as their cause. He was a geographer and astronomer from Massalia who wrote about his voyage to Northern Europe in about 325 BC.

The Coligny calendar was found in 1897 in Coligny, Ain, near Lyon, along with broken pieces of a life-size bronze statue of a nude male holding a spear, likely meant to portray Mars, the Roman god of war. The tablet survives in 73 fragments, and approximately 40% of the original calendar remains. It is now held at the Gallo-Roman Museum of Lyon-Fourvière.

The Coligny calendar reconciles the cycles of the moon and sun. It registers a 5-year cycle of 62 lunar months, each divided into a bright and a dark fortnight. Its notations show that months began with the first quarter moon, and a 13th intercalary month was added every 2.5 years to align the lunations with the solar year.

Among the Insular Celts, the year was divided into a light half and a dark half. As the day began at sunset, the year began with the arrival of darkness at Samhain, around 1 November. The light half started at Bealtaine, around 1 May.

At Aquae Sulis in Roman Britain, engineers drove oak piles into the mud to give the sacred spring a stable foundation, then surrounded it with a lead-lined stone chamber. In the 2nd century the baths were enclosed in a wooden barrel-vaulted building with hot, lukewarm, and cold baths.

Pytheas's own account of his voyage has not survived. What we know comes from later writers such as Strabo, Diodorus of Sicily, and Pliny's Natural History, written in AD 77. They quoted or paraphrased him hundreds of years after his journeys.

The Coligny calendar is written in the Gaulish language using the Latin alphabet and Roman numerals. The plaque dates to the end of the second century CE, but copying errors indicate that the calendar itself is much older.

The Coligny calendar achieves a complex synchronisation of solar and lunar months, which points to a considerable degree of sophistication. Its date of inception is unknown, but correspondences between Insular and Continental Celtic calendars suggest some early form may date to the earlier Iron Age.

Pytheas introduced the idea of distant Thule to the geographic imagination. Not everyone believed him: Strabo said that Dicaearchus did not trust his stories, while Pliny said that Timaeus believed Pytheas's story of the discovery of amber.

The twelve lunar months of the Coligny calendar are reconstructed as Samonios, Dumannios, Rivros, Anagantios, Ogronios, Cutios, Giamonios, Simivisonnios, Equos, Elembivios, Edrinios, and Cantlos. The names appear in the genitive form, such as SAMONI, in the calendar's internal notations.

politics.text: Vercingetorix united most of the Gallic tribes in a great revolt against Rome in 52 BC. He was elected to command a major coalition and aimed to exhaust the Roman forces with scorched-earth tactics, destroying settlements, crops and stores, and with harassment of Caesar's foragers. After his surrender at Alesia, where the refugees the Gauls had expelled from the town died of starvation between the walls and the Roman lines, he was held for six years in the Tullianum, Rome's state prison. In 46 BC he was displayed in Caesar's triumph and then executed in the Tullianum, possibly by strangulation.

The Battle of Alesia in September 52 BC marked the end of Gallic independence in the modern territory of France and Belgium. Caesar's army built two lines of fortifications, an inner wall to keep the besieged Gauls in and an outer wall to keep the Gallic relief force out. They were studded with traps: sharpened stakes arranged so attackers would be impaled, and pits with fire-hardened stakes hidden under twigs. When food ran short, the Gauls sent out their old, sick, wives and children hoping Caesar would take them captive and feed them, but Caesar forbade their admission and Vercingetorix left them between the fortifications to starve to death.

Rome's conquest of Britain began in earnest in AD 43 under Emperor Claudius. By AD 87 it was largely completed in the southern half of the island, most of what is now England and Wales. The conquered territory became the Roman province of Britannia.

Boudica was a queen of the Iceni who led a failed uprising against Rome in AD 60 or 61. Her husband Prasutagus had ruled as a nominally independent ally of Rome, and when he died his will leaving the kingdom jointly to his daughters and the emperor was ignored; the kingdom was annexed and his property taken. According to Tacitus, the Romans pillaged the countryside and ransacked the king's household, and Boudica was flogged and her daughters were raped.

Carausius, a Menapian from Belgic Gaul, was suspected of letting pirates raid the coasts and collect loot before attacking them, then keeping the captured treasure for himself, and Maximian ordered his execution. In late 286 or early 287 he learned of the sentence and answered by declaring himself emperor in Britain and northern Gaul. He held power for seven years, calling himself the 'Emperor of the North', until his finance minister Allectus assassinated him.

Hadrian's Wall was begun in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian and ran from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway. Hadrian ended Trajan's policy of expansion and focused on defending existing borders. Britain had no natural boundary, so a wall was built to divide the Roman province from the Celtic tribes in the north.

Vercingetorix's father Celtillus was murdered around 70 to 60 BC by members of the Arvernian aristocracy, who feared that his attempt to restore kingship in place of the oligarchic system would lead to a more absolute form of rule over the tribe. Sometime between 121 and 70 BC the Arverni had abandoned kingship for an oligarchic system like that of their rivals the Aedui. Vercingetorix himself was later proclaimed king in early 52 BC, after he captured Gergovia with his followers and expelled his opponents.

After Alesia, Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa became the first governor of Gaul in 39 to 38 BC. He built a radial network of roads centred on the Gallic capital, Lugdunum (Lyon), and Gaul was divided into three Roman provinces. Only the Arverni kept their independence, thanks to their victory over Caesar at Gergovia.

Cunobelinus was a king in pre-Roman Britain from about AD 9 to about AD 40, and Suetonius called him 'King of the Britons'. He ruled much of southeastern Britain, including the Catuvellauni and Trinovantes, and used the title Rex and classical motifs on his coins. He may have been a client king of Rome.

Before the invasion of AD 43, Rome kept a balance of power in southern Britain, backing the Catuvellauni and the Atrebates. In 39 or 40 AD Caligula received an exiled Catuvellaunian and planned an invasion that collapsed in farcical circumstances before it left Gaul. Claudius later invaded to aid another fugitive ruler, Verica of the Atrebates.

Augustus prepared invasions of Britain in 34, 27 and 25 BC, but the first and third were called off because of revolts elsewhere in the empire. The second was abandoned because the Britons seemed ready to come to terms. Strabo wrote that Britain paid more in customs and duties than could be raised by taxation if the island were conquered.

Carausius presented himself as reviving traditional Roman virtues and the traditions of the Empire established by Augustus, though he ruled from Britain rather than Rome. He seems to have borrowed a propaganda theme already used by the Tetrarchy, which claimed to have restored a Golden Age and used Virgilian allusions.

philosophy.text: In the Iron Age, Celtic polytheism was the predominant religion in the area now known as England. Worship centred on many gods rather than one, long before Christianity arrived.
Christianity was first established in Britain by the Roman Empire. Archaeological evidence for Christian communities begins to appear in the 3rd and 4th centuries.
According to legend, Christianity was brought to Britain by Joseph of Arimathea, who came to Glastonbury. A separate tradition credits Lucius of Britain with introducing the faith.
The Christian monk Gennadius of Massilia, who died around 496, wrote Of Church Doctrine (De Ecclesiasticis Dogmatibus). The work was long attributed to Saint Augustine.

culture.text: The Celts were a collection of Indo-European peoples identified by their use of Celtic languages and other cultural similarities. Major groups included the Gauls and the Britons, Picts and Gaels of Britain and Ireland. In current scholarship, 'Celt' primarily refers to speakers of Celtic languages, not to a single ethnic group.

The La Tène culture flourished in the late Iron Age, from about 450 BC to the Roman conquest in the 1st century BC. Centered on ancient Gaul, it is often distinguished from earlier cultures mainly by the La Tène style of Celtic art.

According to legend, Christianity was introduced to Britain by Joseph of Arimathea, who came to Glastonbury. Another tradition credits Lucius of Britain with bringing it. The article states that Christianity was first established in Britain by the Roman Empire.
Scholars debate the interrelationships of ethnicity, language and culture in the Celtic world. One open question is in what ways the Iron Age people of Britain and Ireland should be called Celts.

La Tène style artefacts start to appear in Britain around the 4th century BCE, and in Ireland rather later. The style of 'Insular La Tène' art is somewhat different, and migratory movements seem at best only partly responsible for spreading La Tène culture there.
Archaeological evidence for Christian communities in Britain begins to appear in the 3rd and 4th centuries. After the Roman legions withdrew, the Romano-British population remained mostly Christian.

La Tène culture developed under considerable Mediterranean influence from the Greeks in pre-Roman Gaul, the Etruscans and the Golasecca culture. Its artistic style nevertheless did not depend on those influences.

Much of what we know about the Gauls comes from ancient writers. Posidonius described the southern Gauls about 100 BC, and later writers such as Strabo used his work, though the original is lost. Caesar wrote extensively about his Gallic Wars in 58–51 BC.

The Anglo-Saxon invaders and settlers, who began arriving in the 4th century, represented a stark return to pre-Christian religion for Britain. The pre-Christian Germanic religion was practised openly in pockets throughout the country for many decades.
Writing in the 2nd century AD, the Greek author Pausanias said that the Gauls were originally called Celts. He placed them in the remotest region of Europe, on the coast of an enormous tidal sea.
